source_document.body:
Honeywell Aerospace plans to build a $500 million manufacturing facility in Tempe, Arizona, adding production space and bringing more complex machining work in-house as suppliers struggle to keep up with demand.
What’s Related
The 300,000-square-foot factory will expand the company’s existing Tempe campus and is expected to open in late 2028. Honeywell said it will create about 600 permanent jobs over time, with construction adding more than 1,000 local jobs.
The plant will serve commercial aviation and defense customers, including production tied to $15 billion in new program wins for its Control Systems unit. It will also add capacity for defense technologies covered by a supplier agreement signed with the U.S. Department of War in March.
“Demand for technology from Honeywell Aerospace continues to accelerate across both commercial and defense markets, and this major investment ensures we can continue delivering for our customers while unlocking long-term growth for our shareholders,” said Jim Currier, president and CEO of Honeywell Aerospace.
Cutting need for outside suppliers
Some of Honeywell’s suppliers can’t produce enough of the precisely machined parts the company needs. The new plant will allow Honeywell to make more of those parts itself, reducing its reliance on outside suppliers.
The factory will also add production space for aircraft systems that customers have already ordered, including Honeywell’s Assure actuation systems and Attune cooling systems. Chief Financial Officer Josh Jepsen said those orders helped drive the decision to build the plant.
“It gives us more capacity. It gives us the ability to be more vertically integrated, control our own destiny a bit more,” Jepsen said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call.
Built around automation
The Tempe facility will combine modular robotics with automated inspection and digital twins . Honeywell also plans to use AI to help improve production and link manufacturing information through a connected digital system.
Honeywell said the plant will serve as a model for its future factories. It is intended to handle business already awarded while providing room to pursue additional aircraft programs.
Supplier shortages remain a problem
The expansion is part of a larger effort to address supply bottlenecks. In its third-quarter presentation, Honeywell said it had committed to bringing production of about 700 parts in-house, representing $100 million in annual spending. Honeywell didn’t say how much of that work will move to Tempe.
Honeywell’s backlog reached $19.3 billion at the end of the quarter, up 12% from a year earlier. Its earnings release said constraints at a small number of mechanical suppliers were limiting output growth.
